title: Why You Need To Make One Classroom Management Commitment Right Now uccess/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a short, targeted calming technique -- one minute of guided silence and diaphragmatic breathing -- for resetting a classroom's emotional temperature when tension has already built up. He is careful to distinguish it from punishment, insisting it must be framed to students as a mutual mental reset rather than a consequence, and walks through the mechanics: sitting up straight, breathing through the nose for four-to-six second counts, and eventually extending the exhale. He grounds the technique physiologically, noting that slower, deeper breathing triggers the parasympathetic nervous system's calming response, and contrasts classrooms with visibly high ambient tension against the goal of a genuinely calm room. The strategy is framed as a supplement that works regardless of which other SCM strategies a teacher is using, something that can be scheduled at predictable points in the day until it becomes a habit students look forward to.
points: A one-minute strategy of shared silence and diaphragmatic breathing is offered as a fast, low-effort way to reset a classroom's emotional temperature.
The break must be framed explicitly as a mutual mental reset, never as a punishment or reaction to misbehavior, or it loses its calming effect.
Slower, deeper nasal breathing is tied to triggering the parasympathetic nervous system, the body's physiological calming mechanism.
Scheduling the technique at predictable points -- mid-morning, after lunch, before dismissal -- helps it become a habit students come to welcome.
quotes: So what is it? It’s to take a break for one minute of silence. Not as a punishment, mind you. It must never be viewed as a negative reaction to behavior.
Slower and deeper breathing triggers the parasympathetic nervous system, which is the body’s calming mechanism.
Some classrooms I enter to observe teachers give me the jitters, like I’ve had too much coffee.
Mid-morning, after lunch, and right before dismissal are especially effective times.
As it becomes a habit it will be something your students look forward to, a calming recalibration to a happier state of mind and body.
